claim: A 974-bp deletion mutant of the Ptth gene was generated, removing part of the 5′ UTR and almost all coding sequence.
source: The deletion mutant PtthDelete removed part of the 5′ UTR and almost all coding sequence and is a protein null (Figure 1A).
evidence: The manuscript describes the generation of a specific deletion mutant with defined characteristics, supported by molecular validation.

claim: The PTTH deletion was confirmed through PCR analysis at the PTTH locus in genomic DNA samples.
source: We confirmed the PTTH knock-out flies by using PCR (Polymerase Chain Reaction) analysis at the PTTH locus in genomic DNA samples (Figure 1B)
evidence: PCR analysis data shown in Figure 1B validates the genomic deletion.

claim: The PTTH deletion was confirmed by RT-PCR to identify the loss of PTTH transcripts in cDNA samples.
source: by using RT-PCR (Real-time PCR) to identify the loss of PTTH transcripts in cDNA samples (Figure 1C)
evidence: RT-PCR data shown in Figure 1C demonstrates loss of PTTH transcripts.

claim: PTTH immunoreactivity was found in the brain of wild-type and heterozygous flies but was absent in homozygous PtthDelete flies.
source: PTTH immunoreactivity was found in the brain of wild-type and heterozygous flies (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A1, 1A3), but was absent in homozygous PtthDelete flies (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A2).
evidence: Immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A demonstrates protein absence in mutants.

claim: PtthDelete larvae lacking PTTH undergo metamorphosis with about 1 day delay compared with the wild-type control.
source: As the previous study, the PtthDelete larvae lacking PTTH undergo metamorphosis with about 1 day delay compared with the wild-type control (Shimell et al., 2018) (data not shown).
evidence: The claim references a previous study and mentions unpublished data consistent with that study.

claim: PtthDelete adult male and female flies had significantly increased weight compared to wild-type flies.
source: Besides, the PtthDelete adult male and female flies had the significant increased weight than wild-type flies (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Weight measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B demonstrate increased body mass in mutants.

claim: Virgin females losing PTTH had significantly higher copulation rate and shorter latency to copulation than wild-type flies.
source: We found that the virgin female losing PTTH had significantly higher copulation rate and shorter latency to copulation than wild-type flies (Figure 1D–G).
evidence: Behavioral assay data shown in Figure 1D-G demonstrates increased receptivity in PTTH mutants.

claim: PtthDelete flies had higher copulation rate and lower latency to copulation compared to heterozygous null mutant females within 2 days.
source: In addition, the PtthDelete flies had higher copulation rate and lower latency to copulation compared to heterozygous null mutant females within 2 days (Figure 1D, E)
evidence: Behavioral data in Figure 1D-E shows dose-dependent effects of PTTH deletion.

claim: The enhanced virgin female receptivity in PTTH mutants had no relationship with the attractivity or locomotion activity of virgin females.
source: The enhanced virgin female receptivity had no relationship either with the attractivity or with the locomotion activity of virgin females (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–E).
evidence: Control experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C-E rule out alternative explanations.

claim: PTTH deletion regulates virgin female receptivity in a dose-dependent manner.
source: These results suggested that PTTH deletion regulates virgin female receptivity in a dose-dependent manner.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data showing differential effects in heterozygous vs homozygous mutants.

claim: Overexpression through PTTH-Gal4>UAS-PTTH is not sufficient to change female receptivity.
source: However, the overexpression through PTTH-Gal4>UAS-PTTH is also not sufficient to change female receptivity (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Behavioral data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A shows no effect of PTTH overexpression.

claim: Decreased expression of PTTH through PTTH-Gal4>UAS-PTTH-RNAi or dsx-Gal4>UAS-PTTH-RNAi did not result in the similar phenotype to that of PTTHDelete/PTTHDelete.
source: Similarly, decreased expression of PTTH through PTTH-Gal4>UAS-PTTH-RNAi or dsx-Gal4>UAS-PTTH-RNAi did not result in the similar phenotype to that of PTTHDelete/PTTHDelete (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B, C).
evidence: Behavioral data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B-C shows RNAi knockdown is insufficient to phenocopy the null mutant.

claim: Neuron-specific expression of PTTH using elav-Gal4 could restore the enhanced copulation rate and shorter latency to copulation in PTTHDelete/PTTHDelete virgin females.
source: We found that neuron-specific expression of PTTH could restore the enhanced copulation rate and shorter latency to copulation in PTTHDelete/PTTHDelete virgin females (Figure 1H).
evidence: Genetic rescue experiment data shown in Figure 1H demonstrates that neuronal PTTH expression rescues the mutant phenotype.

claim: PTTH neurons are a pair of bilateral neurosecretory cells in the brain directly innervating the prothoracic gland during the larval stage.
source: The labeled neurons were the same as reported before (McBrayer et al., 2007; Yamanaka et al., 2013), a pair of bilateral neurosecretory cells in the brain directly innervating the prothoracic gland during the larval stage (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Anatomical labeling data in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A confirms the identity and projection pattern of PTTH neurons, consistent with prior literature.

claim: Newly emerged flies had similar PTTH neuron anatomical pattern to that of the larval stage.
source: The newly emerged flies had the similar anatomical pattern with that of the larval stage (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Anatomical imaging data in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B shows persistence of PTTH neuron pattern after eclosion.

claim: The pattern of PTTH neurons labeled by Ptth-Gal4>UAS-mCD8GFP gradually could not be found after the 10th hour after eclosion.
source: However, while the prothoracic gland cells are gradually degenerating during pharate adult development (Dai and Gilbert, 1991; Roy et al., 2018), the pattern of PTTH neurons labeled by Ptth-Gal4>UAS-mCD8GFP gradually could not be found after the 10th hour after eclosion (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Time-course imaging data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2 shows disappearance of PTTH neuron labeling after 10 hours post-eclosion, consistent with prothoracic gland degeneration reported in cited studies.

claim: All PTTH neurons are doublesex-positive.
source: Double labeling of dsx-LexA and Ptth-Gal4 neurons (LexAop-tomato,UAS-stinger-GFP/Ptth-LexA;dsx-Gal4/+) revealed that PTTH neurons are all doublesex-positive (Figure 2C).
evidence: Double-labeling experiment data shown in Figure 2C demonstrates complete overlap between PTTH and dsx expression.

claim: All PTTH neurons express both Ptth and Dsx, as shown by intersectional strategy.
source: We then used an intersectional strategy to visualize overlapped expression between dsx-LexA and Ptth-Gal4 (UAS > stop > myrGFP/+;LexAop2-FlpL,dsx-LexA/Ptth-Gal4). We observed all PTTH neurons with GFP signals (Figure 2D).
evidence: Intersectional genetic labeling data in Figure 2D confirms co-expression of Ptth and Dsx in all PTTH neurons.

claim: Decreasing DsxF expression in PTTH neurons did not significantly change female receptivity.
source: We decreased the DsxF expression in PTTH neurons and did not detect significantly changed female receptivity (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Behavioral data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C shows no effect of DsxF knockdown in PTTH neurons.

claim: Activating PTTH neurons transiently in adult virgin females at 29°C did not significantly change copulation rate or latency to copulation.
source: First, we activated PTTH neurons transiently in adult virgin females by driving the temperature-sensitive activator dTrpA1 (Hamada et al., 2008) using Ptth-Gal4. PTTH neurons were activated at 29°C compared with the control treatment at 23°C. No significantly different copulation rate or latency to copulation was detected (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A–C).
evidence: Thermogenetic activation experiment data in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A-C shows no effect of adult PTTH neuron activation on receptivity.

claim: PTTH neurons do not regulate virgin female receptivity during the adult stage.
source: This suggested that PTTH neurons do not regulate virgin female receptivity during the adult stage.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the thermogenetic activation experiment showing no effect in adults.

claim: When PTTH neurons were inactivated during the larval stage, this was the only situation when the controls were both different from the experimental group.
source: When the experiment was done at the larval stage is the only situation when the controls were both different from the experimental (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Temporal inactivation experiment data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D shows specific effect during larval stage.

claim: When PTTH neurons were inactivated during whole pupal or whole adult stages, virgin female copulation rate did not change significantly.
source: However, when PTTH neurons were inactivated during whole pupal or whole adult stages, virgin female copulation rate did not change significantly (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Temporal inactivation experiment data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D shows no effect during pupal or adult stages.

claim: The copulation rate did not change significantly when activating PTTH neurons during stage 1, 3, or 4.
source: The copulation rate did not change significantly when activating PTTH neurons during the stage 1, 3, or 4 (Figure 3B, D, E).
evidence: Temporal activation experiment data in Figure 3B, D, E shows no effect during these developmental stages.

claim: Activating PTTH neurons during stage 2 resulted in significantly lower copulation rate and longer latency to copulation.
source: However, we found the significant lower copulation rate and the longer latency to copulation only when PTTH neurons were activated during the stage 2 (Figure 3C, F).
evidence: Temporal activation experiment data in Figure 3C, F shows specific effect during stage 2 (third instar to wandering stage).

claim: The defected copulation when PTTH neurons were activated during stage 2 was not due to lower locomotion activity of virgin females.
source: The defected copulation was not due to a lower locomotion activity of virgin females (Figure 3G).
evidence: Locomotion assay data in Figure 3G rules out locomotor defects as an explanation.

claim: The activity of dsx+ PTTH neurons negatively regulates virgin female receptivity during the stage from the start of the third instar to the end of wandering stage.
source: Taken together, our findings indicated that the activity of dsx+ PTTH neurons negatively regulate virgin female receptivity during the stage from the start of the third instar to the end of wandering stage.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the temporal activation experiments.

claim: The enhanced copulation rate and shorter latency to copulation of PtthDelete flies were rescued to the comparable level of wild-type females by feeding 20E to third-instar larvae.
source: The enhanced copulation rate and shorter latency to copulation of the PtthDelete flies were rescued to the comparable level of wild-type females (Figure 4).
evidence: 20E feeding rescue experiment data in Figure 4 demonstrates that ecdysone mediates PTTH's effect on receptivity.

claim: Wild-type females fed by 20E had no significantly different copulation rate and latency to copulation compared with wild-type females fed by 95% ethanol.
source: Furthermore, the wild-type females fed by 20E had no significantly different copulation rate and latency to copulation compared with the wild-type females fed by the same volume of 95% ethanol which is the solvent of 20E (Figure 4).
evidence: Control experiment data in Figure 4 shows 20E feeding alone does not affect wild-type receptivity.

claim: PTTH regulates virgin female receptivity through the titer of ecdysone.
source: This suggested that PTTH regulates virgin female receptivity through the titer of ecdysone.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the 20E rescue experiment.

claim: EcR-A and EcR-B1 express in both pC1 and vpoDN neurons.
source: The GFP signals labeled by pC1-ss2-Gal4 and vpoDN-ss1-Gal4 were merged well with the signals of both EcR-A and EcR-B1 antibodies, respectively (Figure 5—figure supplement 1). This revealed that EcR-A and EcR-B1 express in both pC1 and vpoDN neurons.
evidence: Immunohistochemistry data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1 shows co-localization of EcR isoforms with pC1 and vpoDN neurons.

claim: Reducing the expression of all EcR isoforms in pC1 neurons decreased the copulation rate and prolonged the latency to copulation significantly.
source: First, we reduced the expression of all EcR isoforms in pC1 neurons, this decreased the copulation rate and prolonged the latency to copulation significantly (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: RNAi knockdown experiment data in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A shows effect of pan-EcR knockdown in pC1 neurons.

claim: Reducing the expression of EcR-A in pC1 neurons resulted in significantly lower copulation rate and longer latency to copulation.
source: Furthermore, we reduced the expression of EcR-A in pC1 neurons. The virgin female had the significant lower copulation rate and longer latency to copulation (Figure 5A).
evidence: RNAi knockdown experiment data in Figure 5A shows effect of EcR-A knockdown in pC1 neurons.

claim: The reduced copulation rate when EcR-A was knocked down in pC1 neurons had no relationship with the attractivity and locomotion activity of virgin females.
source: The reduced copulation rate had no relationship with the attractivity (Figure 5E) and the locomotion activity of virgin females (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Control experiments in Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 2B rule out alternative explanations.

claim: Reducing the expression of EcR-B1 in pC1 neurons resulted in significantly longer latency to copulation but comparable copulation rate to controls.
source: When reducing the expression of EcR-B1 in pC1 neurons, virgin females had the significant longer latency to copulation but the comparable copulation rate to controls (Figure 5B).
evidence: RNAi knockdown experiment data in Figure 5B shows partial effect of EcR-B1 knockdown in pC1 neurons.

claim: Reducing the expression of EcR-A and EcR-B1 in vpoDN neurons did not affect virgin female receptivity.
source: However, reducing the expression of EcR-A (Figure 5—figure supplement 3A–C) and EcR-B1 (Figure 5—figure supplement 3D–F) using three split vpoDN-Gal4s in vpoDN neurons all did not affect virgin female receptivity.
evidence: RNAi knockdown experiment data in Figure 5—figure supplement 3A-F shows no effect of EcR knockdown in vpoDN neurons.

claim: The expression of EcR-A in pC1 neurons regulates virgin female copulation rate, but EcR isoforms in vpoDN neurons do not modulate virgin female receptivity.
source: This suggested that the expression of EcR-A in pC1 neurons regulates virgin female copulation rate, but EcR isoforms in vpoDN neurons do not modulate virgin female receptivity.
evidence: This is an interpretation summarizing the differential effects of EcR knockdown in different neuron types.

claim: When EcR-A or EcR-B1 were reduced in pC1-a, -c, and -e neurons simultaneously using pC1-ss1-Gal4, the copulation rate or the latency to copulation did not change significantly.
source: We also tested virgin female receptivity when EcR-A or EcR-B1 were reduced in pC1-a, -c, and -e neurons simultaneously using pC1-ss1-Gal4, respectively. While the copulation rate or the latency to copulation did not change significantly (Figure 5C, D).
evidence: RNAi knockdown experiment data in Figure 5C, D shows no effect when specific pC1 subtypes are targeted.

claim: pC1b only, or both pC1b and pC1d neurons is necessary for the functions of EcR-A and EcR-B1 in pC1 neurons on virgin female receptivity.
source: This suggested that, pC1b only, or both pC1b and pC1d neurons is necessary for the functions of EcR-A and EcR-B1 in pC1 neurons on virgin female receptivity.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparing effects of different pC1 subtype-specific manipulations.

claim: Reducing EcR-A in pC1d neurons alone did not significantly change virgin female receptivity including copulation rate and latency to copulation.
source: However, when reducing EcR-A in pC1d neurons alone using the specific split-Gal4 SS56987 (Schretter et al., 2020), virgin female receptivity including copulation rate and latency to copulation did not change significantly compared with controls (Figure 5—figure supplement 4).
evidence: RNAi knockdown experiment data in Figure 5—figure supplement 4 shows no effect of EcR-A knockdown specifically in pC1d neurons.

claim: The function of EcR-A in pC1b neurons is necessary for virgin female copulation rate.
source: These results suggested that the function of EcR-A in pC1b neurons is necessary for virgin female copulation rate.
evidence: This is an inference based on the pattern of effects across different pC1 subtype manipulations.

claim: Manipulation of EcR-A did not enhance egg laying significantly in virgin females.
source: We found that manipulation of EcR-A did not enhance egg laying significantly in virgin females (Figure 5F), although the UAS-EcR-A-RNAi control causes a massive decrease in female fertility.
evidence: Egg laying assay data in Figure 5F shows no increase in egg laying when EcR-A is knocked down in pC1 neurons.

claim: Reducing EcR-A expression in pC1 neurons leads to significantly less VPO and more OE.
source: Meanwhile, we further analyzed whether reduction of EcR-A in pC1 neurons regulates the VPO or the OE. We found that reducing the EcR-A expression in pC1 neurons lead to the significantly less VPO and more OE (Figure 5G, H).
evidence: Behavioral analysis data in Figure 5G, H shows specific effects on VPO and OE behaviors.

claim: Reduced EcR-A expression in pC1 neurons results in a similar phenotype to that of mated females.
source: These results suggested that reduced EcR-A expression in pC1 neurons results in the similar phenotype to that of mated females.
evidence: This is an interpretation comparing the behavioral phenotype to known mated female behavior.

claim: When the experiment was done at the pupal stage, this was the only situation when the controls were both different from the experimental group for EcR-A knockdown.
source: When the experiment was done at the pupal stage is the only situation when the controls were both different from the experimental (Figure 5J).
evidence: Temporal knockdown experiment data in Figure 5J shows specific effect during pupal stage.

claim: EcR-A in pC1 neurons plays a role in virgin female receptivity during metamorphosis.
source: The result suggested that EcR-A in pC1 neurons plays a role in virgin female receptivity during metamorphosis.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the temporal knockdown experiments.

claim: The morphology of pC1-ss2-Gal4 expressing neurons appeared after the formation of the white pupa.
source: First, we tested the morphology of pC1 neurons when reducing the expression of EcR-A in pC1 neurons. We found that the morphology of pC1-ss2-Gal4 expressing neurons appeared after the formation of the white pupa (Figure 6A1).
evidence: Developmental imaging data in Figure 6A1 shows timing of pC1 neuron morphology appearance.

claim: Reduced EcR-A expression induced more elaborated morphologies of pC1-d/e cells, especially the extra vertical projection (EVP) near the midline of brains.
source: The reduced EcR-A expression induced the more elaborated morphologies of the pC1-d/e cells, especially the extra vertical projection (EVP) near the midline of brains (Figure 6B–D; Deutsch et al., 2020).
evidence: Anatomical imaging data in Figure 6B-D shows morphological changes in pC1 neurons when EcR-A is reduced.

claim: The morphological changes in pC1 neurons when EcR-A was reduced exhibited from the second day of the pupal stage and maintained at the adult stage.
source: These changes exhibited from the second day of the pupal stage (Figure 6B1, B2, E) and maintained at the adult stage (Figure 6D1, D2, F).
evidence: Time-course imaging data in Figure 6B, D, E, F shows persistence of morphological changes from pupal to adult stage.

claim: The number of pC1 cell bodies in adult flies when EcR-A was reduced were the same as that of wild-type flies.
source: Meanwhile, the number of pC1 cell bodies in adult flies when EcR-A was reduced were the same as that of wild-type flies (Figure 6G).
evidence: Cell counting data in Figure 6G shows no change in pC1 neuron number.

claim: The abnormal development of pC1d neurons may induce changes between pC1d neurons and other dsx+ and fru+ neurons to affect associated behaviors.
source: Previous studies suggested that pC1d cells serve as a hub within the central brain for dsx+ and fru+ neurons (Deutsch et al., 2020). Thus, the abnormal development of pC1d neurons may induce the changes between pC1d neurons and other dsx+ and fru+ neurons to affect associated behaviors.
evidence: This is a speculation based on prior literature about pC1d connectivity and the observed morphological changes.

claim: Reduced EcR-A did not induce significantly different calcium responses in the LPC.
source: Reduced EcR-A did not induce significantly different calcium responses in the LPC (Figure 6H).
evidence: Calcium imaging data in Figure 6H shows no change in basal neural activity when EcR-A is reduced.

claim: The decreased female copulation rate induced by reduced EcR-A in pC1 neurons was mainly due to the morphological changes of pC1b neurons, which then modulate the connections of pC1b neurons with other neurons.
source: Thus, our results suggested that the decreased female copulation rate induced by reduced EcR-A in pC1 neurons was mainly due to the morphological changes of pC1b neurons, which then modulate the connections of pC1b neurons with other neurons.
evidence: This is an interpretation integrating the morphological and functional data.

claim: PTTH deletion induced upregulated EcR-A compared with PTTH heterozygous flies during the start of prepupa stage.
source: We quantified the EcR-A expression in the whole pupa body during the start of prepupa stage, when the pC1-ss2-Gal4 expressing neurons appear. Indeed, PTTH−/− induced upregulated EcR-A compared with PTTH−/+ flies (Figure 7A).
evidence: qRT-PCR data in Figure 7A shows increased EcR-A expression in PTTH mutants.

claim: There is a feedforward relationship between PTTH and EcR-A expression during the start of prepupa stage.
source: This suggested the feedforward relationship between PTTH and EcR-A expression during the start of prepupa stage.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the EcR-A expression data in PTTH mutants.

claim: When PTTH was deleted, pC1 neurons exhibited a contradictory pattern to that when EcR-A was decreased in pC1 neurons.
source: Consistent with this, when PTTH was deleted, pC1 neurons exhibited the contradictory pattern to that when EcR-A was decreased in pC1 neurons (Figure 7B, C).
evidence: Anatomical imaging data in Figure 7B, C shows opposite morphological changes in PTTH mutants vs EcR-A knockdown.

claim: The feedforward relationship between PTTH and EcR-A may explain the contradictory functions of PTTH deletion and EcR-A reduction in pC1 neurons for female receptivity.
source: These suggested the feedforward relationship between PTTH and EcR-A, and may explain the contradictory functions of PTTH deletion and EcR-A reduction in pC1 neurons for female receptivity.
evidence: This is an interpretation connecting the molecular and behavioral observations.

claim: There is slightly overlap of dsx-LexA>LexAop-RFP and torso-Gal4>UAS-GFP during larval stage.
source: Indeed, we detected the slightly overlap of dsx-LexA>LexAop-RFP and torso-Gal4>UAS-GFP during larval stage (Figure 7D).
evidence: Double-labeling imaging data in Figure 7D shows partial overlap between torso and dsx expression.

claim: Decreasing torso expression in pC1 neurons significantly inhibits female receptivity.
source: Furthermore, decreasing torso expression in pC1 neurons significantly inhibit female receptivity (Figure 7E).
evidence: RNAi knockdown experiment data in Figure 7E shows effect of torso knockdown in pC1 neurons.

claim: The inhibited virgin female receptivity when torso was decreased in pC1 neurons had no relationship with the locomotion activity of virgin females.
source: The inhibited virgin female receptivity had no relationship either with the locomotion activity of virgin females (Figure 7F).
evidence: Locomotion assay data in Figure 7F rules out locomotor defects as an explanation.

claim: PTTH regulates female receptivity not only through ecdysone, but also may through regulating other neurons especially DsxF-positive neurons associated with female receptivity directly.
source: These results suggest that, PTTH regulates female receptivity not only through ecdysone, but also may through regulating other neurons especially DsxF-positive neurons associated with female receptivity directly.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the torso knockdown results suggesting direct PTTH signaling to pC1 neurons.

claim: Peptide hormone PTTH negatively modulates virgin female receptivity through ecdysone.
source: In this study, we found that peptide hormone PTTH negatively modulates virgin female receptivity through ecdysone.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main finding integrating multiple experimental results.

claim: PTTH neurons are doublesex-positive and regulate virgin female receptivity during neural development.
source: PTTH neurons are doublesex-positive and regulate virgin female receptivity during neural development.
evidence: This is a summary statement integrating the anatomical and temporal manipulation data.

claim: PTTH deletion resulted in the increased ecdysone receptor EcR-A expression in newly formed prepupae.
source: PTTH deletion resulted in the increased ecdysone receptor EcR-A expression in newly formed prepupae.
evidence: This is a summary of the qRT-PCR results.

claim: EcR-A functions in pC1 neurons to positively regulate virgin female receptivity during metamorphosis mainly through modulating the anatomical morphology of pC1b neurons.
source: Furthermore, EcR-A functions in pC1 neurons to positively regulate virgin female receptivity during metamorphosis mainly through modulating the anatomical morphology of pC1b neurons.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation integrating the temporal, anatomical, and functional data.

claim: Decreasing the expression of PTTH receptor torso in pC1 neurons inhibited female receptivity.
source: Additionally, decreasing the expression of PTTH receptor torso in pC1 neurons inhibited female receptivity.
evidence: This is a summary of the torso knockdown results.

claim: The PG axis has similar functional strategy as the hypothalamic–pituitary–gonadal axis in mammals to trigger the juvenile–adult transition.
source: The PG axis has similar functional strategy as the hypothalamic–pituitary–gonadal axis in mammals to trigger the juvenile–adult transition.
evidence: This is a comparative statement drawing on established knowledge about mammalian and insect endocrine systems.

claim: This work suggests a general mechanism underlying which the neurodevelopment during maturation regulates female sexual receptivity.
source: Our work suggests a general mechanism underlying which the neurodevelopment during maturation regulates female sexual receptivity.
evidence: This is a broad interpretive claim about the general significance of the findings.

claim: Female sexual receptivity is essential for reproduction of a species.
source: Female sexual receptivity is essential for reproduction of a species.
evidence: This is a general statement based on established biological knowledge.

claim: Neuropeptides play the main role in regulating female receptivity.
source: Neuropeptides play the main role in regulating female receptivity.
evidence: This is a general statement based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: Sexually mature adult virgin females validate males after sensing the courtship song and male-specific sex pheromone, receive courtship with pausing and opening the vaginal plate (VPO).
source: Sexually mature adult virgin females validate males after sensing the courtship song and male-specific sex pheromone, receive courtship with pausing and opening the vaginal plate (VPO) (Ferveur, 2010; Greenspan and Ferveur, 2000; Hall, 1994; Wang et al., 2021).
evidence: This describes established Drosophila courtship behavior supported by multiple citations.

claim: If the female is not willing to mate, she may kick her legs, flick her wings, or extrude the ovipositor to deter males.
source: If the female is not willing to mate, she may kick her legs, flick her wings, or extrude the ovipositor to deter males (Connolly and Cook, 1973).
evidence: This describes established Drosophila rejection behavior supported by citation.

claim: Mated females reject males for several days after mating mainly through more ovipositor extrusion (OE) and less VPO.
source: Mated females reject males for several days after mating mainly through more ovipositor extrusion (OE) and less VPO (Fuyama and Ueyama, 1997; Wang et al., 2021).
evidence: This describes established post-mating behavior in Drosophila supported by citations.

claim: doublesex (dsx) and fruitless (fru) are the terminal genes in sex determination regulatory hierarchy.
source: doublesex (dsx) and fruitless (fru) are the terminal genes in sex determination regulatory hierarchy.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Drosophila sex determination.

claim: dsx and fru specify nearly all aspects of somatic sexual differentiation, including the preparation for sexual behaviors.
source: They specify nearly all aspects of somatic sexual differentiation, including the preparation for sexual behaviors (Dickson, 2008; Manoli et al., 2013; Manoli et al., 2006; Mellert et al., 2012; Pavlou and Goodwin, 2013; Siwicki and Kravitz, 2009; Yamamoto, 2007; Yamamoto and Koganezawa, 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: In males, expression of male-specific FruM is important for male courtship behaviors.
source: In males, expression of male-specific FruM (Billeter et al., 2006; Demir and Dickson, 2005; Hall, 1978; Manoli et al., 2005; Stockinger et al., 2005) and male-specific DsxM (Kohatsu et al., 2011; Pan and Baker, 2014; Pan et al., 2011; Rideout et al., 2010) is important for male courtship behaviors.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: In females, neurons with DsxF or fru P1 promoter regulate some aspects of the female sexual behaviors.
source: In females, although functional Fru protein is not translated, neurons with DsxF or fru P1 promoter regulate some aspects of the female sexual behaviors (Kvitsiani and Dickson, 2006; Rideout et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Fru and dsx are involved in regulating the sexual dimorphism during neurodevelopment.
source: Fru and dsx are involved in regulating the sexual dimorphism during neurodevelopment (Yamamoto and Koganezawa, 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The sexual dimorphism of P1 and mAL neurons is the result of regulation by Dsx and/or Fru.
source: For instance, the sexual dimorphism of P1 and mAL neurons which are all associated with male courtship and aggression behaviors (Clowney et al., 2015; Hoopfer et al., 2015; Kimura et al., 2008; Kohatsu et al., 2011; Pan et al., 2012; Sengupta et al., 2022; von Philipsborn et al., 2011) is the result of regulation by Dsx and/or Fru (Ito et al., 2012; Kimura et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: During postembryonic development, the PG axis triggers the juvenile–adult transition, similar to the function of hypothalamic–pituitary–gonadal (HPG) axis in mammals.
source: During postembryonic development, the PG axis triggers the juvenile–adult transition, similar to the function of hypothalamic–pituitary–gonadal (HPG) axis in mammals (Herbison, 2016; Pan and O'Connor, 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge about comparative endocrinology supported by citations.

claim: Hormones of the PG axis act to transform the larval nervous system into an adult version.
source: Hormones of the PG axis act to transform the larval nervous system into an adult version (Truman and Riddiford, 2023).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Ecdysone is the prime mover of insect molting and metamorphosis and is involved in all phases of neurodevelopment, including neurogenesis, pruning, arbor outgrowth, and cell death.
source: Ecdysone belonging to the PG axis is the prime mover of insect molting and metamorphosis and is involved in all phases of neurodevelopment, including neurogenesis, pruning, arbor outgrowth, and cell death (Truman and Riddiford, 2023).
evidence: This is established knowledge about ecdysone function supported by citation.

claim: Neurons read the ecdysteroid titer through two isoforms of the ecdysone receptor, EcR-A and EcR-B1, according to spatial and temporal conditions in the CNS.
source: The neurons read the ecdysteroid titer through two isoforms of the ecdysone receptor, EcR-A and EcR-B1, according to spatial and temporal conditions in the central nervous system (CNS) (Riddiford et al., 2000; Truman et al., 1994).
evidence: This is established knowledge about ecdysone receptor function supported by citations.

claim: EcR-A is required in fru P1-expressing neurons for the establishment of male-specific neuronal architecture.
source: EcR-A is required in fru P1-expressing neurons for the establishment of male-specific neuronal architecture, and ecdysone receptor deficient males display increased male–male courtship behavior (Dalton et al., 2009; Ganter et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: In virgin females, dsx+ pCd neurons respond to the cVA, while dsx+ pC1 neurons also respond to male courtship song.
source: In virgin females, dsx+ pCd neurons respond to the cVA, while dsx+ pC1 neurons also respond to male courtship song (Zhou et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Receptive females open the vaginal plate (VPO) through activation of the dsx+ vpoDN neurons.
source: The receptive females open the vaginal plate (VPO) through activation of the dsx+ vpoDN neurons (Wang et al., 2021).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: After mating, sex peptide in the seminal fluid binds to the fru+ dsx+ sex peptide sensory neurons in the female uterus.
source: After mated, sex peptide in the seminal fluid binds to the fru+ dsx+ sex peptide sensory neurons in the female uterus. Then neuronal activity in the dsx+ sex peptide abdominal ganglion neurons of the ventral nerve cord and in the pC1 neurons is reduced (Avila et al., 2011; Feng et al., 2014; Häsemeyer et al., 2009; Kubli, 2003; Wang et al., 2020b; Yang et al., 2009; Zhou et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge about post-mating signaling supported by multiple citations.

claim: Sexual receptivity is reduced with less VPO and more OE which is controlled by dsx+ DpN13 neurons.
source: Therefore, the sexual receptivity is reduced with less VPO and more OE which is controlled by dsx+ DpN13 neurons (Wang et al., 2020a).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The neuropeptides Drosulfakinin, myoinhibitory peptides and SIFamide are involved in female sexual receptivity.
source: The neuropeptides Drosulfakinin, myoinhibitory peptides and SIFamide are involved in female sexual receptivity (Jang et al., 2017; Terhzaz et al., 2007; Wang et al., 2022).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Dopamine, serotonin, and octopamine are pivotal to female sexual behaviors.
source: As monoamines, dopamine, serotonin, and octopamine are pivotal to female sexual behaviors (Ishimoto and Kamikouchi, 2020; Ma et al., 2022; Neckameyer, 1998; Rezával et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The identified neuropeptides and monoamines modulating female sexual receptivity all function during the adult stage.
source: So far, the identified neuropeptides and monoamines modulating female sexual receptivity all function during the adult stage.
evidence: This is a summary of established knowledge in the field.

claim: PTTH is a brain-derived neuropeptide hormone and is the primary promoter of the synthesis of steroid hormone 20-hydroxyecdysone (20E).
source: PTTH, a brain-derived neuropeptide hormone, is the primary promoter of the synthesis of steroid hormone 20-hydroxyecdysone (20E) (McBrayer et al., 2007; Rewitz et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge about PTTH function supported by citations.

claim: pC1 neurons encode the mating status of females.
source: Because 20E acts through its receptor EcR (Riddiford et al., 2000), we then tested the function of EcR in pC1 neurons which encode the mating status of females (Zhou et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.
